newsitem.title: Belgium: Delhaize sees global market, local stomachs.
newsitem.headline: Delhaize sees global market, local stomachs.

text.p: The world may be becoming a global supermarket forcing food retailers to merge, but it remains one of local tastes that cannot be ignored, the head of Belgium's second largest retailer, Delhaize, said on Wednesday.

"Think global but act local," Delhaize chief executive officer Gui De Vaucleroy told a seminar of Belgian financial analysts. "We must increasingly have a global strategy but never forget that food products are a local business."
Retailers, particularly in the food sector, must pay close attention to the demands and lifestyles of their consumers wherever they were, he said.
"More than ever the food distributor must adapt to local habits and lifestyles," De Vaucleroy said.
In the United States in particular supermarkets had ignored the growth in convenience foods and paid the price.
"We call this the market of the stomach," he said, noting that in the United States and some parts of Europe the average time spent on food preparation in the home was just 15 minutes per day.

But at the same time, with most so-called mature markets of the United States and Western Europe experiencing slow or no growth, retailers were increasingly being forced to look to other horizons for their business.
De Vaucleroy singled out Latin America and Asia, particularly the South East as key areas for expansion.
He said that Delhaize, already well established in the United States through its Food Lion chain, was looking for places and local partners in Asia.

"I hope that in the coming months we will be present in Asia. We have studies under way. It is our intention in Asia to work with local partners," he said without detailing which countries were being scrutinised or if any specific partners had been identified.
De Vaucleroy said that alliances rather than straight takeovers would play a rising part in the of the retail sector as it coped with increasing globalisation.
"Food distribution is not capital rich, and alliances can give the same benefits as takeovers but without having to pay the premiums," he said.
De Vaucleroy said the retail sector would continue to concentrate on the emerging tiger economies as mature economies slowed, and the need to curb costs and get economies of scale.

"It is indisputably the case that it is becoming increasingly difficult to find good commercial sites..Therefore there will be a push towards more concentration to the detriment of smaller businesses," he said.
He noted that in the United States in particular, but also in parts of Europe, the annual increase in retail sales space outstripped both the rise in the population and in the standard of living.
At the same time, increasingly supply of goods was falling into the hands of fewer giant companies which meant that the supermarket chains were facing tougher price negotiations.
